title: Orbital AI Data Centers Run Into a Physics Wall, JPL Analysis Finds
excerpt: A NASA JPL preprint argues cooling, radiator mass and launch scale make general-purpose AI computing in orbit uneconomic, even as Google, SpaceX and Starcloud push ahead.
body:
• A new arXiv analysis by Dr Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory argues orbital AI data centers fail on physics before they fail on ambition: cooling, mass and launch scale.
  • A 1-megawatt orbital facility — roughly a small server room — would need 5,640 square metres of solar panels and 2,500 square metres of radiators, and weigh an estimated 34 to 59 metric tons.
  • Matching AI demand growth would take an estimated 170,000 to 461,000 small orbital units in five years, implying almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches; launch cost alone runs about $3,360 per kilogram against the $250-$1,000 per kilogram the economics require.
  • Google's Project Suncatcher, SpaceX's FCC-approved Starmind plan and Starcloud's 88,000-satellite filing are proceeding anyway; the paper concedes niches such as Earth-observation processing and collision avoidance.

The pitch is seductive: put AI data centers in orbit, where sunlight is constant, land is free and no planning board can object. A new preprint by Dr Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, examined by Universe Today, argues the industry is building that pitch on back-of-the-envelope arithmetic — and that the physics, worked through properly, is prohibitive at any useful scale.

The cooling problem comes first

Space is cold, but it has no air. Conduction and convection — the ways Earth data centers shed heat — do not exist in a vacuum, so every watt of computing heat must be radiated away from dedicated panels. IEEE Spectrum's analysis of the same physics puts the scale plainly: a single 700-watt Nvidia H100 chip needs about 1.4 square metres of radiator to hold 60 degrees C, and a standard 40-kilowatt AI rack needs an 80-square-metre radiator, roughly a pickleball court. Radiation and ultraviolet exposure degrade radiator coatings, so after five years the same chip needs nearly 2 square metres — about 40% more area, and 40% more mass, launched on day one.

Mass is where the economics break

Turyshev's baseline is a 1-megawatt orbital facility, about the computing power of a small commercial server room. In a dawn-dusk orbit chosen to minimise time in Earth's shadow, it would still need 5,640 square metres of solar panels — about an American football field — plus 2,500 square metres of radiators. With structure, thrusters and shielding, the paper estimates 34 to 59 metric tons for that single megawatt. Shrinking to 100-kilowatt units of roughly 5 tons each does not rescue the plan: keeping pace with demand would require launching an estimated 170,000 to 461,000 of them over five years, at up to four per Falcon 9 — almost 9,000 launches, or about 33 a week.

The cost comparison is starker. A high-end terrestrial AI data center costs $10,000 to $40,000 per kilowatt of capacity. For an orbital system at 40 kilograms per kilowatt to match that, launch and manufacturing together would have to cost $250 to $1,000 per kilogram; a dedicated Falcon 9 launch today works out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram, three to thirteen times the entire allowable budget. ABI Research's separate comparison, cited by IEEE Spectrum, reached a similar order of magnitude: running a GPU in space for a year costs at least ten times the terrestrial figure. Data return adds a third constraint — optical downlinks advertise 200 gigabits per second but sustain roughly 13 to 26 gigabits, only in line of sight and never through cloud — and cosmic rays steadily flip bits and degrade both chips and panels.

The industry is proceeding anyway

None of this has slowed the announcements. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared at GTC in March that "space computing, the final frontier, has arrived." Google's Project Suncatcher, with Planet, plans two TPU-carrying test satellites by early 2027, and Google has booked a Blue Origin flight for a Suncatcher test. Starcloud has filed with the FCC for an 88,000-satellite orbital data center constellation, and on November 25 the FCC approved SpaceX's application to launch one million "Starmind" orbital data centers by 2040.

Turyshev's paper does leave the door open where the physics points the other way: processing Earth-observation data in orbit and downlinking only the conclusions, and onboard collision avoidance for a low Earth orbit already holding more than 17,000 satellites. In those niches the computer sits next to the sensor and the data never has to make the trip down. General-purpose AI training in orbit, the analysis concludes, is a different matter — the wall is not engineering effort but thermodynamics and mass, and it will be a long time before either moves.
